text: "The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch." The verb means divinely called. After Acts, the epistles never call believers disciples.
explanation:
In the Gospels and Acts, followers of Jesus are disciples, students, just as Gamaliel and other rabbis had disciples. Then in Antioch something new happened. The word for "called" is chrematizo, used elsewhere when God warned Joseph in a dream and revealed to Simeon that he would see the Christ. Young's Literal Translation renders it: "the disciples also were divinely called first in Antioch Christians."

After Acts, not one letter to the churches uses the word disciple. We never stop learning; we're lifelong students of grace. But don't let anyone tell you that being a Christian is the basic level and being a disciple is the higher calling. God Himself named you Christian: anointed one, a son or daughter in His family.

text: Paul never called Timothy "my disciple." He called him "my true son in the faith."
explanation:
Paul clearly trained Timothy. Yet the language is family, not school: "my beloved son." A rabbi's disciples often had to leave their families to follow him; in God's family, sonship includes being taught but is far more than that.

"You therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. And the things that you have heard from me… commit these to faithful men who will be able to teach others also." Count the links: Jesus to Paul, to Timothy, to faithful men, to others. Five, the number often linked with grace. And notice God looks for faithful people first; the ability to teach follows.

text: The older brother was a son, yet he said, "These many years I have been serving you." He had a son's place but a slave's heart.
explanation:
He came in from the field, heard music and dancing, and refused to go in. "Lo, these many years I have been serving you; I never transgressed your commandment at any time; and yet you never gave me a young goat." Not "Father," not "my brother," but "this son of yours." Scripture calls him the older son, huios, yet he related to his father as an employee keeping score.

The father gently answered, "Son, you are always with me, and all that I have is yours." Bitterness and self-righteousness are rarely cured by trying harder to be nice. The root is a lost sense of sonship. "You are no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then an heir."

text: A butterfly that lands among rubbish is still a butterfly. It doesn't turn back into a caterpillar.
explanation:
You may fall into old habits, addictions or dark moods, but you aren't defined by them. If you're in Christ, you're a new creation. Preaching doesn't tell you who you are to make you that; it tells you because that's who you already are.

When temptation or depression says, "This is the real you," it's coming from outside, trying to get in, not rising from your true nature. The Egyptians lie dead on the shore behind you. Reckon it so: "This isn't who I am. I'm the righteousness of God in Christ." Get up, shake yourself off, and fly.

text: "Why are you praying to Me like that? I'm your Father. Talk to Me like a son."
explanation:
During a stressful season, Joseph Prince found himself praying intensely: "God, please, God, I need this done!" Then he sensed the Holy Spirit's gentle correction, and with it a revelation of sonship. He'd slipped from "Father" to "God," from family to distance, from rest to strain.

Sometimes just saying "Father" a few times restores everything. He may have revealed Himself as El Shaddai, Yahweh and El Elyon, but "Father" is the name Jesus came to reveal. A son doesn't beg for what's already in the family fridge. "Father, You want this for me more than I do. Thank You, I receive it."

text: Luke 14 ends with Jesus thinning a crowd who wanted a teacher. Luke 15 opens with sinners drawing near to a Saviour.
explanation:
"Great multitudes went with Him," and Jesus turned and spoke of hating father and mother and carrying a cross. Those listening were happy to collect good teaching from another impressive rabbi. Jesus wanted them to see they needed far more: to pass through death into life.

The very next verse: "Then all the tax collectors and the sinners drew near to Him to hear Him." They didn't come to admire His teaching; they came because they needed Him. A drowning man doesn't need a book on swimming; he needs someone to pull him out. The parables of grace that follow tell you why He saves: there's joy in heaven over every lost one found.

text: At the Last Supper, eleven asked, "Lord, is it I?" Judas alone said, "Rabbi, is it I?"
explanation:
When Jesus said one of them would betray Him, "each of them began to say to Him, 'Lord, is it I?'" Judas said, "Rabbi, is it I?" To the end, Jesus was only a teacher to him.

Earlier, when Jesus said that no one could come to Him unless the Father drew them, "many of His disciples went back and walked with Him no more." It's John 6:66. They wanted a teacher who'd improve them, not a Saviour who'd humble them. Jesus asked the twelve, "Do you also want to go away?" Peter answered, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."
